Farmers weigh the cost of new tariffs

Growers say the harvest is fine; the market is not.

Published on 29 Oct 2026

When Ruth Calder looks across her soybean fields in the county, she sees the best harvest in a decade, and a crop she may not be able to sell at a profit.

New tariffs on exports, announced in the spring, have cut the price buyers will pay by almost a fifth, according to figures from the state's farm bureau.

Read more: The new tariffs explained in five charts

Calder, who farms 600 acres with her brother, said the family had borrowed against the land to buy seed and fertiliser, as it does every year, and now faces a growing debt.

We did everything right this year, and it still might not be enough to keep the farm, she said.

Economists say the effects are uneven. Large operations can store grain and wait for prices to recover, while smaller farms often have to sell at harvest to pay their bills.

The agriculture department has promised relief payments, but farmers say the money has been slow to arrive and will cover only part of their losses this season.
